name: Garland Hensley
languages: Army French (enough to buy bread, and to apologise)
equipment: Heavy coat: his olive-drab Army greatcoat from 1918, the brass buttons swapped for horn
Service revolver, a .38 issued by the Ironwood Detective Agency, with IDA stamped on the frame
Pump shotgun, agency issue, kept in the guards' shanty at the drift mouth between shifts
An Ironwood Detective Agency badge, No. 27, and a commission as a special deputy of Selden County signed by Sheriff Boyd Sizemore
A five-cell electric flashlight and a police whistle
His Army discharge, his Victory Medal with two battle clasps, and a letter from his mother asking him please to come home for Sunday dinner even if he has to wear that badge
A pint of Mingo County moonshine, half gone
features: Been Here Before (Survivor origin: advantage on initiative; when a fight or a fright begins he always knows the nearest way out of the place he is in; once per long rest, rerolls a failed saving throw, including a fear check; the first time each scenario he meets a horror like the one he survived, the GM tells him one way it is the same. He survived eleven hours in a collapsed dugout in the Argonne in the dark with two dead men.)
Held the Line (Veteran: advantage on fear checks while a conscious ally is within 10 ft of him; once per short rest, when Panic would take him, he acts normally instead)
Drill: Close Quarters (Veteran: no disadvantage on ranged attacks with a sidearm or a shotgun against a creature within 5 ft of him; it changes nothing written on the sheet)
Second Wind (Veteran, 2nd level: once per short rest, as a bonus action, regains 1d10 + 3 hit points, and loses 1 Dread if he is at Dread 3 or higher)

Service: Sapper (Veteran, 3rd level: 1st Engineers, AEF; proficient with dynamite, which he can set, fuse and disarm safely; thrown dynamite he lights uses DC 8 + proficiency + DEX. He knows what blasting powder does in a closed space with gas in it, and he will say so.)

Nobody's Business (Drifter background: seven years on freights and back roads since the war; he knows where to sleep for nothing, which towns run strangers out, and how to travel without a ticket; when a drifter goes missing nobody asks, and he has been that drifter)

personality.traits: I'm easy company and I make everybody laugh, and I drink a little more than I let on. I sit with my back to a wall. I call every older woman in the camp ma'am and every older man by his first name, the way I did when I was a boy here.
personality.ideals: I told myself it's just a job: five dollars a day to walk a tipple and carry a gun. I told myself that a man who's been through what I've been through has a right to look after himself. I'm finding out I don't believe it.
personality.bonds: My mother, Dovie Hensley, in a company house on Number Two Bottom, who says she'll be evicted before she'll take a penny of my pay. My brother Rad, who is in the union and won't speak to me. Lester Gaither, who walked the tipple with me on the night of 25 March, and who I left alone for ten minutes.
personality.flaws: I go along. I always have: with the Army, with the freight crews, with Captain Kincaid. I am afraid of the dark in a way I have never told a living soul, and I'll do almost anything not to be alone in it.

appearance: A lanky, sandy-haired man of thirty-one with a long weathered face, a crooked grin, pale blue eyes, a front tooth chipped by a rifle butt in 1918, and a habit of rubbing his left wrist. Army greatcoat over a guard's khaki, a badge he keeps forgetting to pin straight, a flashlight on his belt that he never, ever lets go out.
backstory: Garland Hensley was born in Ottway in 1896, in the second company house on Number Two Bottom, the son of a coal loader killed by a slate fall when Garland was twelve. He went into the mine at seventeen, hated it, and enlisted in 1917 to get out. He came home from France in 1919 with a medal and a thing about the dark, worked one month at No. 3, and was in 4 South on 14 October 1919 when 7 North blew; he carried two burned men out to the drift mouth and walked off the job the next morning and did not come back for seven years. He rode freights from Seattle to Mobile. This February, broke in Charleston, he saw that the Ironwood Detective Agency was hiring guards for the southern coal camps at five dollars a day, and when they said Ottway he said yes before he could think about it. His mother will not take his money. His brother crossed the road rather than speak to him. On the night of 25 March he walked the tipple shift with Lester Gaither, a Navy man from Huntington and the only guard he liked, and they split up at the coal bins for ten minutes so Garland could go and smoke where Captain Kincaid couldn't see. When he came back, Lester's flashlight was lying on the tipple boards, switched on, its beam pointing at the drift mouth, and Lester was gone. Two union men are in the Gale jail for his murder. Garland knows they were home in bed. He has not said so.
